newsitem.title: ALBANIA: ALBANIA FEELS PINCH FROM GREEK FARM BLOCKADE.
newsitem.headline: ALBANIA FEELS PINCH FROM GREEK FARM BLOCKADE.

text.p: A two-week Greek farmers' protest blocking domestic transport is starting to pinch the economy of neighbouring Albania, traders and customs officials said on Wednesday.

Sali Hiri, chief customs officer in southern town of Gjirokaster near the border with Greece, said imports from Greece, especially food, building materials, drinks, fuel and detergents, had dropped by 90 percent.

"And the 10 percent of imports from Greece that are getting through cost around 150 to 200 percent more than normal because truck drivers are forced to use secondary roads to avoid the roadblocks," Hiri told Reuters.
His figures were confirmed by Greek customs officials, who said Greece-bound passenger traffic had dropped by 80 percent.
Some items are beginning to disappear from shop shelves.
Greece is Albania's second trading partner, and accounted for more than 20 percent of imports during 1995 and 21 percent in the first half of 1996.
Greek farmers have erected nearly 100 road blocks using thousands of tractors in their protest for cheaper fuel, equipment and higher prices. The Greek government refuses to bow to their demands.
Albanian exporters in Gjirokaster stopped despatching trucks to Greece since the blockade started.
A local company said one of its trucks took three days to reach Gjirokaster from Athens along rural routes, a trip that normally takes six hours on the motorway.

"Detergents, sausages and pasta are disappearing from some shops in Gjirokaster and in others the prices of these items have gone up by 10 percent," said Sedat Qeribashi of Gjirokaster's Chamber of Commerce.

Drinks company chief Kosta Sotiri said many consumers had not yet felt the pinch because his firm was using up stocks, but added: "If the blockade continues until Christmas...then no doubt we will have empty shelves for the festivities."

Nevruz Culli, a meat inspector who checks imports at the Kakavija border pass, 25 km (12 miles) south of Gjirokaster, said the six meat deliveries from Greece per day had stopped since the protest began.
Albanians raising livestock had also begun to complain about a shortage of animal feed from Greece, he said.
